summary: The article provides a generally accurate overview of anchor investors in Indian IPOs, with most factual claims verified against authoritative sources. However, some details regarding the Jio Platforms IPO and the latest SEBI regulations on anchor investor allocation are either slightly off or presented in a way that could be misleading without further clarification.

claims.claim: Anchor investors commit large sums, typically ₹10 crore or more for mainboard IPOs, to show confidence in the company.
claims.note: SEBI regulations mandate a minimum investment of ₹10 crore for mainboard IPOs for anchor investors.

claims.claim: To ensure commitment, their shares are locked in for two periods: 50% for 30 days and the rest for 90 days.
claims.note: SEBI mandates a lock-in period of 30 days for 50% of the shares allotted to anchor investors and 90 days for the remaining 50% from the date of allotment.

claims.claim: SEBI's updated rules for anchor investors, especially concerning their lock-in periods, came into effect from April 2022 and were further refined around November 2025, ensuring continued relevance of this topic.
claims.note: The dual lock-in period (50% for 30 days, 50% for 90 days) for anchor investors was made effective for issues opening on or after April 1, 2022. Further refinements to the anchor investor framework, including expanded reservations, were introduced around November 2025.

claims.claim: For a mainboard IPO (larger companies), the minimum investment is ₹10 crore, while for an SME IPO (smaller companies), it's ₹2 crore.
claims.note: SEBI regulations specify a minimum investment of ₹10 crore for mainboard IPOs and ₹2 crore for SME IPOs for anchor investors.

claims.claim: A portion of the IPO, specifically carved out from the QIB category, is reserved for anchor investors. This can be up to 60% of the QIB portion. To encourage domestic participation, one-third (33.33%) of this anchor portion is reserved for domestic mutual funds.
claims.note: Anchor investors can be allotted up to 60% of the QIB portion, and one-third (33.33%) of this anchor portion is reserved for domestic mutual funds.

claims.claim: Recently, large IPOs like Jio Platforms, which closed its public subscription in late October 2026, had significant anchor investor participation. The lock-in period for the first half of the shares allotted to anchor investors in such recent IPOs is ending around late November 2026, bringing their role and the associated rules back into focus.
claims.note: Jio Platforms IPO public subscription closed on October 23, 2026. The 30-day lock-in period for 50% of anchor investor shares for Jio Platforms is expected to end around November 24, 2026.

claims.claim: If the final IPO price (decided after public bidding) is higher than the anchor price, the anchor investor pays the difference. If it's lower, they don't get a refund and still pay their original, higher anchor price.
claims.note: If the final issue price is higher than the anchor price, anchors pay the difference. If it is lower, they do not get a refund and are allotted at the anchor price.

claims.claim: For SME IPOs, the minimum is ₹2 crore.
claims.note: The minimum investment for an SME IPO by an anchor investor is ₹2 crore.

article_title: Your IPO Just Got a 'Big Investor' Stamp of Approval: Understanding Anchor Investors
